content: Leukorrhea, also spelled leucorrhoea in Commonwealth English, refers to a thick, whitish vaginal discharge. This condition typically arises due to inflammation or congestion of the vaginal mucosa. If the discharge appears yellowish or emits an unpleasant odor, it is important to consult a healthcare provider, as this may indicate the presence of a sexually transmitted disease (STD). In many cases, leukorrhea is a normal physiological sign that the vagina is healthy and self-cleaning. It can sometimes occur before a girl experiences her first menstrual period, serving as an indicator of the onset of puberty. There are numerous causes of leukorrhea, with one of the most common being an increase in estrogen levels. The volume of discharge may also increase in the presence of vaginal infections or STDs, which can cause the discharge to become yellow and malodorous. It is important to note that vaginal discharge is a normal occurrence in women, and its characteristics can vary significantly among individuals. Changes in the nature of the discharge may be attributed to infections, malignancies, or hormonal fluctuations. Leukorrhea is also commonly observed during pregnancy. This is due to increased blood flow to the vaginal tissues, which is driven by elevated estrogen levels. Additionally, female infants may experience leukorrhea for a brief period after birth as a result of in-utero exposure to maternal estrogen. In most cases, leukorrhea is a non-pathological symptom secondary to inflammatory conditions affecting the vagina or cervix. However, postpartum leukorrhea accompanied by back pain and foul-smelling lochia (a vaginal discharge containing blood, mucus, and placental tissue following childbirth) may indicate uterine involution failure. This condition, where the uterus does not return to its pre-pregnancy size, is often associated with an underlying infection.
